extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, film students, producers, and anyone learning screenplay format/style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing, formatting, presenting, and registering screenplays and teleplays for film, television, and related media. Covers typographic, physical, stylistic, and industry-practical criteria that distinguish professional scripts from amateur work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-per-minute rule
rubrics_metrics.description: One page of properly formatted screenplay is a ballpark estimate for roughly one minute of screen time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule of thumb is widely used (e.g., for estimating runtime) but is contested — dialogue-heavy pages often take less screen time than action-heavy pages and runtime depends on writer style and production choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard font and typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard font is 12 point, 10 pitch Courier typeface; studio format also stipulates font size and line spacing for screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the standard Courier-typeface conventions helps preserve page-to-minute estimates and signals professionalism. Many screenwriting references (e.g., 'Hollywood Standard Formatting') and writing competitions expect these conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins and page geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide margins of at least one inch are employed (usually larger on the left for hole punches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Margins aid readability and leave space for production notes; left margin is often wider to accommodate brads or binding. Physical paper size and margin treatment differ by country (see US/UK physical format).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action writing (screen direction) — present tense and limited scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is written in the present tense and limited to what can be heard or seen by the audience (descriptions of settings, character movements, sound effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include internal thoughts or non-observable exposition. Keep action concise and cinematic; historically, continuity scripts included detailed shot lists, but modern master-scene scripts favor readability and only necessary visual cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is written in a center column and consists of the words the characters speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical matter and character names have specific placement rules in studio format. Overuse of parentheticals or stage directions inside dialogue is discouraged as unprofessional or intrusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slug lines / master scene headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Each scene begins with a slug line (master scene heading) typically containing INT. or EXT., the specific location, and the time of day; each slug line begins a new scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slug lines make scene boundaries explicit for readability and production planning. In a shooting script, slug lines are often numbered consecutively for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slug line numbering for shooting scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: In a shooting script, the slug lines are numbered consecutively for ease of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbering scenes eases shooting logistics, scheduling, and communication with production departments; this is a feature of the technical shooting script rather than the readable master-scene script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio format standardized elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Studio format stipulates how elements such as scene headings, action, transitions, dialogue, character names, shots and parenthetical matter should be presented on the page, as well as font size and spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single universal standard but most mainstream studios expect a 'studio format'. Competitions and contracts may specify exact formatting. References: The Complete Guide to Standard Script Formats, Nicholl Fellowship guide, The Hollywood Standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical format — United States
rubrics_metrics.description: American screenplays are printed single-sided on three-hole-punched US letter-size paper (8.5 × 11 in) and held with two brass brads in the top and bottom holes (middle hole left empty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripts are usually bound with a light card stock cover and back page; covers protect the script during handling. Physical delivery conventions remain in many contracts despite electronic distribution becoming common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical format — United Kingdom (and other non-US considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the UK, double-hole-punched A4 paper is normally used; some British writers format for US letter size when sending to American producers to avoid cropping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: British scripts may be bound with a single brad at top-left to ease page-flicking during meetings. When sending across borders, electronic copies or cropping to US letter are common practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading copies and electronic delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading copies (distributed to attract finance or talent) may be printed on both sides, professionally bound, or reduced to half-size for convenience; electronic copies are common for delivery and copyright documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic delivery facilitates copyright registration and documenting authorship date. Reduce paper waste with double-sided reading copies; production crew or director may prefer reduced-size or bound copies during shooting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and copyright practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can register works with the Writers Guild of America West (WGAW) Registry and the US Copyright Office; registration affects remedies in infringement cases (e.g., statutory damages and attorneys fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registering with WGAW and/or the Copyright Office documents authorship and can preserve legal remedies. In the UK copyright is automatic, but registration may help when dealing with overseas producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative screenplay (spec script) expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A spec screenplay (spec script) is written to be sold on the open market with no upfront payment; content is usually invented solely by the screenwriter though can be based on existing works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spec scripts are judged by marketability and craft, and are submitted in the same studio format conventions; competitions and coverage often evaluate spec scripts against professional-format and storytelling criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television format differences (act breaks and sitcom formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: American TV hour-long dramas and single-camera sitcoms use similar format rules to motion pictures but include act breaks; multi-camera sitcoms use a different format derived from stage plays and radio (double-spaced dialogue, capitalized action lines, capitalized/underlined scene headings and sound effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV scripts require explicit act breaks for network scheduling and pacing. Multi-camera sitcom format reflects live-audience/stage origins and uses unique typographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary and audio-visual two-column format
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary scripts or presentations that consist largely of voice-over matched to images use a two-column format (audio/video), different from standard single-column screenplay formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-column formats are harder to edit in standard word processors, so many script-editing programs include templates for documentary formats. Use appropriate templates for voice-over/image synchronization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of screenwriting software to enforce conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Various screenwriting software packages (e.g., Final Draft, Celtx, Fade In, Movie Magic Screenwriter, WriterDuet, Scrivener) help writers adhere to strict formatting conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software eases correct placement of scene headings, dialogue, parentheticals, pagination, and export. Use industry-standard packages when submitting to producers or competitions to avoid formatting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script coverage as an evaluative rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Script coverage is the analysis and grading of screenplays (often within production companies) that usually takes the form of a written report guided by a rubric that varies by company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage summarizes the project, breaks down its elements, and suggests whether the producer should consider producing it; rubrics may include assessments of story, character, commercial viability, and technical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master-scene script vs shooting script distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Master-scene scripts include all dialogue but only rudimentary scene descriptions, prioritizing readability; shooting scripts (devised after approval) contain detailed technical instructions and numbered slug lines for production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and financiers often prefer readable master-scene scripts for evaluation, while directors and production crews use shooting scripts for logistics. The shift from continuity-heavy scripts to master-scene elevated readability but reduced technical specificity in initial drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting signals professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper adherence to screenplay formatting conventions is a way of distinguishing a professional from an amateur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting errors can lead to negative reception regardless of story quality. Competitions, producers, and agencies often expect adherence to studio format as a baseline professional signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding, covers and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripts are usually bound with light card stock cover and back pages (often showing production company or agency logo) to protect them during handling; physical binding conventions differ by region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good physical presentation reduces wear during circulation and signals professional care; include appropriate cover information and protect the script when sending to multiple readers.
